title: Recognizing the power and promise of Social Security at 90
summary: Happy 90th birthday to Social Security! But at a time when 10,000 Americans a day are retiring, we need to make sure the trust fund is healthy and operations are fully funded to keep providing benefits for many more years, writes Hank Greenberg.
content:
by Hank Greenberg, Maryland Matters August 14, 2025

by Hank Greenberg, Maryland Matters August 14, 2025

Today, Social Security – the vital lifeline for tens of millions of Americans everywhere, including 1.1 million Marylanders, used for housing, groceries, gas and the other everyday necessities – is marking its 90th birthday.

And with that anniversary comes a responsibility to strengthen the program – and determine how we can help it age in the healthiest way. As the bedrock of retirement in America, our financial future depends on protecting Social Security for decades to come.

Social Security will face challenges in the years ahead, but it’s incumbent on us to ensure the program continues to work for the 67 million Americans across the country who rely on it. The history of the program shows us how necessary it is for the healthy retirement of Americans everywhere.

On Aug. 14, 1935, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act, and in January 1935 Ida M. Fuller, the first person to receive Social Security, collected a monthly check of $22.54—that’s $518.58 in inflation-adjusted dollars. From that beginning, the program now provides $1.4 trillion in retirement security. It is the only inflation-adjusted retirement program, and it guarantees that Americans everywhere know they can plan soundly for retirement.

Here in Maryland, more than 1.1 million residents collect Social Security benefits, and 186,000 are lifted out of poverty every month. Social Security helps Marylanders live and retire with dignity, offers crucial support to those with disabilities and serves as a financial lifeline for families navigating the loss of a loved one.

Social Security will never “go broke.” That’s a fact. Social Security is a pay-as-you-go system. As long as there are workers paying into Social Security, there will be Social Security for those collecting benefits. The program is funded by payroll taxes, and will continue to pay benefits.

But the program does face funding challenges. The most recent Social Security Trustees’ Report finds that the surplus will run out in 2035, if not sooner. To prevent that shortfall, Congress must once again step up – as it did when it reformed the program in 1983 – before millions of Americans face a 20% loss in earned benefits.

Customer service is another area where Social Security is facing challenges, with office closures and staffing shortages. Many Americans who need access to the program face long wait times on the on the phone or long distances to reach local offices.

This year, wait times are on the rise, fewer people can reach a Social Security representative to meet their needs and this challenge emerges just as more people – approximately 10,000 people every day – are retiring.

Congress must provide SSA with the resources necessary to provide timely, efficient and effective customer service. And Congress needs to provide oversight to ensure that customer service is prioritized.

Throughout our history at AARP, we have worked with every administration and Congress to advocate for the protection of Social Security. More than 67 million Americans everywhere rely on this vital program, and for 90 years, Social Security has been the foundation of retirement in the United States. It’s imperative to ensure that Social Security remains not just for another 90 years, but for generations to come.
